source_text: Quoquo tamen, inquis, modo substantia creatoris delicti capax inuenitur, cum adflatus dei, id est anima, in homine deliquit nec potest non ad originalem summam referri corruptio portionis. ad hoc interpretanda erit qualitas animae. inprimis tenendum quod Graeca scriptura signauit, adflatum nominans, non spiritum. quidam enim de Graeco interpretantes non recogitata differentia nec curata proprietate uerborum pro adflatu spiritum ponunt et dant haereticis occasionem spiritum dei delicto infuscandi, id est ipsum deum. et usurpata iam quaestio est. intellege itaque adflatum minorem spiritu esse. ut aurulam eius, et si de spiritu accidit, non tamen spiritum. nam et aura uento rarior, et si de uento aura, non tamen uentus. [aura] capit etiam imaginem spiritus dicere flatum. nam et ideo homo imago dei, id est spiritus; deus enim spiritus. imago ergo spiritus flatus. porro imago ueritati non usquequaque adaequabitur. aliud est enim secundum ueritatem esse, aliud ipsam ueritatem esse. sic et adflatus, cum imago sit spiritus, non potest ita imaginem dei comparare, ut, quia ueritas, id est spiritus, id est deus, sine delicto est, ideo et imago, id est adflatus, (id est homo,) non debuerit admisisse delictum. in hoc erit imago minor ueritate et adflatus spiritu inferior, habens illas utique lineas dei, qua inmortalis, [anima] qua libera et sui arbitrii, qua praescia plerumque, qua rationalis, capax intellectus et scientiae, tamen et in his imago et non usque ad ipsam uim diuinitatis; sic nec usque ad integritatem a delicto, quia hoc soli deo cedit, id est ueritati.
thought_title: The Nature of the Creator's Substance
pass_a_gloss: However, you ask, in what way is the substance of the creator found to be capable of sin, since the breath of God, that is the soul, sins in man and the corruption of the part cannot be referred back to the original sum except that the quality of the soul is to be interpreted. First, it must be held that the Greek scripture has designated, naming breath, not spirit. For some, interpreting from Greek, not considering the difference nor the property of words, put spirit in place of breath and give heretics the opportunity to obscure the spirit of God with sin, that is God himself. And the question has already been taken over. Understand therefore that breath is less than spirit. Just as breeze is rarer than wind, and if breeze comes from wind, it is not however wind. For breeze can also be called the image of spirit, breath. For man is the image of God, that is spirit; for God is spirit. Therefore, the image of spirit is breath. Furthermore, the image will not be entirely equal to the truth. For it is one thing to be according to truth, another to be the truth itself. So also breath, since it is the image of spirit, cannot compare to the image of God in such a way that, because truth, that is spirit, that is God, is without sin, therefore the image, that is breath, (that is man,) ought not to have admitted sin. In this, the image will be less than the truth and breath inferior to spirit, having indeed those lines of God, in that it is immortal, in that it is free and of its own will, in that it is often prescient, in that it is rational, capable of intellect and knowledge, yet even in these, the image and not up to the very power of divinity; so also not up to the integrity from sin, because this yields only to God, that is truth.

choices.why: to refer to God or the divine

pass_b_english: You're asking how the creator's substance can be capable of sin when it's the breath of God - the soul - that sins in humans, and the corruption of a part can't be traced back to its original source without considering the soul's nature. The key to understanding this lies in the Greek scripture, which specifically refers to 'breath', not 'spirit'. Some translators, however, have failed to appreciate the distinction between these terms and have used 'spirit' instead of 'breath', giving heretics an opportunity to tarnish God's spirit with sin - essentially, to tarnish God Himself. This question has already been hijacked, so let's set the record straight: breath is less than spirit. To illustrate the point, consider that a breeze is a lighter version of the wind, and just as a breeze can originate from the wind without being the wind itself, so too can breath be seen as an image or echo of spirit. After all, humans are made in the image of God, who is spirit, so it follows that the image of spirit is breath. But here's the crucial thing: an image will always fall short of the real thing - it's one thing to reflect the truth, but quite another to be the truth itself. So, while breath may be the image of spirit, it can't be expected to replicate God's sinless nature, simply because God is truth incarnate. The image of God, as reflected in humans, carries certain divine attributes - immortality, freedom, self-awareness, rationality, and the capacity for knowledge - yet these qualities are always going to be imperfect reflections, lacking the full power of divinity, and therefore susceptible to sin, which is something that only God, as the embodiment of truth, can avoid.

review.notes: Pass B is a paraphrase/summary rather than a translation. It omits the specific logical structure of the comparison between 'aura' and 'ventus' (wind) and the specific list of divine attributes (prescience/prescientia) found in the Latin and Pass A. Most importantly, Pass B fails the completeness requirement by transforming the text into a modern commentary style ('let's set the record straight', 'here's the crucial thing', 'it's one thing to reflect...') and omitting the specific clause 'non debuerit admisisse delictum' (ought not to have admitted sin) in favor of a general statement about being 'susceptible to sin'.
reasons: Pass B is a paraphrase/summary, not a translation. It adds interpretive filler ('let's set the record straight', 'here's the crucial thing') and omits the specific logical connection regarding the 'ought not' (non debuerit) in the comparison of the image to the truth. It also omits the specific attribute of 'prescience' (praescia) present in the Latin and Pass A.
